summary: Describes lig, the LISP Internet Groper, a simple tool for querying the LISP mapping database to see which routing locators belong to an endpoint identifier. It is the LISP counterpart of everyday diagnostic tools. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP splits addresses into two kinds: an endpoint identifier used inside a site, and a routing locator used out on the Internet. 'lig' is a command that asks the mapping database which locators serve a given endpoint identifier, and prints the answer. It is the LISP equivalent of asking a DNS server where a name points.

subtitle: A command that asks a LISP mapping database which locators serve a given endpoint identifier.

tldr.problem: LISP splits addresses into endpoint identifiers used inside a site and routing locators used on the Internet, so an operator who wants to check a mapping has to query a distributed database rather than look at a routing table.
tldr.mechanism: The 'lig' command sends a Map-Request for a destination endpoint identifier and prints the reply: the matched EID-prefix, the locators with their up/down status, priority and weight, and a round-trip time estimate.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document describing a diagnostic tool rather than a new protocol, and it also explains how to check whether a site has registered properly with a Map-Server.

facts.label: Endpoint ID size
facts.value: 32 bits for IPv4, 128 bits for IPv6

today: RFC 6835 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It describes a diagnostic command rather than a new protocol, and it was written while LISP was still being deployed on a pilot network, so its description of that deployment is a snapshot of the time.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol specifies an architecture and mechanism for replacing the addresses currently used by IP with two separate namespaces: Endpoint IDs, used within sites, and Routing Locators, used on the transit networks that make up the Internet infrastructure. To achieve this separation, LISP defines protocol mechanisms for mapping from EIDs to RLOCs. In addition, LISP assumes the existence of a database to store and propagate those mappings globally. Several such databases have been proposed, among them a Content distribution Overlay Network Service for LISP, a Not-so-novel EID-to-RLOC Database, and LISP Alternative Topology, with LISP+ALT being the system that was being implemented and deployed on the pilot LISP network at the time of writing.

In conjunction with the various mapping systems, there exists a network-based API called the LISP Map-Server. Using Map-Resolvers and Map-Servers allows LISP sites to query and register into the database in a uniform way independent of the mapping system used. Sending Map-Requests to Map-Resolvers provides a secure mechanism to obtain a Map-Reply containing the authoritative EID-to-RLOC mapping for a destination LISP site.

The 'lig' is a manual management tool to query the mapping database. It can be run by all devices that implement LISP, including Ingress Tunnel Routers, Egress Tunnel Routers, Proxy-ITRs, Proxy-ETRs, Map-Resolvers, Map-Servers and LISP-ALT Routers, as well as by a host system at either a LISP-capable or non-LISP-capable site. The mapping database system is typically a public database used for wide-range connectivity across Internet sites, and the information in the public database is purposely not kept private so it can be generally accessible for public use.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP splits addresses into two kinds: an endpoint identifier used inside a site, and a routing locator used out on the Internet. 'lig' is a command that asks the mapping database which locators serve a given endpoint identifier, and prints the answer. It is the LISP equivalent of asking a DNS server where a name points.

sections.title: The Terms 'lig' Works With
sections.content:
A Map-Server is a network infrastructure component that learns EID-to-RLOC mapping entries from an authoritative source, typically an ETR, though static configuration or another out-of-band mechanism may be used, and advertises these mappings in the distributed mapping database. A Map-Resolver accepts LISP Encapsulated Map-Requests, typically from an ITR, quickly determines whether or not the destination IP address is part of the EID namespace, and if it is not, immediately returns a Negative Map-Reply. Otherwise it finds the appropriate EID-to-RLOC mapping by consulting the distributed mapping database system.

A Routing Locator is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of an Egress Tunnel Router, and it is the output of an EID-to-RLOC mapping lookup. An EID maps to one or more RLOCs. Typically RLOCs are numbered from topologically aggregatable blocks that are assigned to a site at each point to which it attaches to the global Internet, so RLOCs can be thought of as Provider-Assigned addresses. Multiple RLOCs can be assigned to the same ETR device or to multiple ETR devices at a site.

An Endpoint ID is a 32-bit value for IPv4 or a 128-bit value for IPv6, used in the source and destination address fields of the first, most inner, LISP header of a packet. The host obtains a destination EID the same way it obtains a destination address today, for example through a DNS lookup, and the source EID is obtained via existing mechanisms used to set a host's local IP address. An EID is allocated to a host from an EID-prefix block associated with the site where the host is located, and EIDs must not be used as LISP RLOCs. EID blocks may be assigned in a hierarchical manner, independent of the network topology, to facilitate scaling of the mapping database.

An Ingress Tunnel Router accepts an IP packet with a single IP header, treats the inner IP destination address as an EID and performs an EID-to-RLOC mapping lookup. It then prepends an outer IP header with one of its globally routable RLOCs in the source address field and the result of the lookup in the destination address field. An Egress Tunnel Router accepts an IP packet where the destination address in the outer IP header is one of its own RLOCs, strips the outer header and forwards the packet based on the next IP header found. ETR functionality does not have to be limited to a router device: a server host can be the endpoint of a LISP tunnel as well.

Two storage structures must not be confused. The EID-to-RLOC Cache is a short-lived, on-demand table in an ITR that stores, tracks, and is responsible for timing out and otherwise validating EID-to-RLOC mappings. The EID-to-RLOC Database is a global distributed database containing all known EID-prefix to RLOC mappings, where each potential ETR typically holds a small piece of it: the mappings for the EID prefixes behind that router.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things have to be kept apart. A cache on each router holds the few mappings that router recently used and expires them. The database is the shared, global record of every site's mappings, and each router only holds its own part of it.

sections.title: What 'lig' Does and Shows
sections.content:
When the 'lig' command is run, a Map-Request is sent for a destination EID, and when a Map-Reply is returned the contents are displayed to the user. The information displayed includes the EID-prefix for the site that the queried destination EID matches; the locator address of the Map Replier; the Locator-Set for the mapping entry, which includes the locator address, up/down status, priority and weight of each Locator; and a round-trip-time estimate for the Map-Request and Map-Reply exchange.

A possible syntax for a 'lig' command is lig <destination> [source <source>] [to <map-resolver>], where the destination is either a Fully Qualified Domain Name or a destination EID for a remote LISP site, the source is an optional source EID to be inserted in the Source EID field of the Map-Request, and the map-resolver is an optional FQDN or RLOC address for a Map-Resolver.

The utility has two use cases. The first is the query described above. The other is to verify whether a site has registered successfully with a Map-Server, which is called 'ligging yourself'. It happens as follows: in the 'lig' initiator, a Map-Request is sent for one of the EIDs for the initiator's own site, and the Map-Request is then returned to one of the ETRs for that site. In response, a Map-Reply is sent back to the locator address of the initiator, the Map-Reply is processed, and the mapping data for the initiator's site is displayed. For host-based implementations within a LISP site, 'lig self' is less useful, since the host may not have an RLOC with which to receive a Map-Reply. But 'lig' can be used in a non-LISP site, as well as from infrastructure hosts, to get mapping information.
sections.plainLanguage: You give it a name or an address, and it prints which locators serve it, whether each is up, its priority and weight, and how long the round trip took. The other use is to check your own site: ask about one of your own addresses and see whether the answer comes back.

sections.title: Implementations and Testing the ALT
sections.content:
The Cisco LISP prototype implementation has support for 'lig' for IPv4 and IPv6. The command line description is lig <dest-eid> [source <source-eid>] [to <mr>] [count <1-5>]. This command initiates the LISP Internet Groper. It is similar to the DNS analogue 'dig' but works on the LISP mapping database. When it is invoked, the local system will send a Map-Request to the configured Map-Resolver, and when a Map-Reply is returned its contents will be displayed to the user. By default, up to three Map-Requests are sent if no Map-Reply is returned, but once a Map-Reply is returned no other Map-Requests are sent. The destination can take a DNS name, or an IPv4 or IPv6 EID address. The source EID can be one of the EID addresses assigned to the site in the default Virtual Routing and Forwarding table. When a Map-Resolver is not configured, the Map-Request is sent on the ALT network if the local router is attached to the ALT.

'Ligging yourself' is accomplished with lig {self | self6} [source <source-eid>] [to <mr>] [count <1-5>]. The destination EID address for the Map-Request will be the first configured EID-prefix for the site with the host bits set to 0. If the Map-Resolver and Map-Server are the same LISP system, then 'lig self' is testing whether the Map-Resolver can turn back a Map-Request to the site. If another Map-Resolver is used, it can test that the site's EID-prefix has been injected into the ALT infrastructure, in which case the Map-Request is processed by the Map-Resolver and propagated through each ALT-Router hop to the site's registered Map-Server, which then returns the Map-Request to the originating site, and an xTR there sends a Map-Reply to the source of the Map-Request. 'lig self6' tests for registering of IPv6 EID-prefixes.

There is also a public domain implementation that can run on any x86-based system, whose only requirement is that the system initiating 'lig' must have an address assigned from the locator namespace. Its syntax is lig [-d] <eid> -m <map-resolver> [-c <count>] [-t <timeout>], where -d prints additional protocol debug output, the count is the number of Map-Requests to send before the first Map-Reply is returned, with a default value of 3 and a range from 1 to 5, and the timeout is the amount of time in seconds before another Map-Request is sent when no Map-Reply is returned, with a default value of 2 seconds and a range from 1 to 5.

Section 5 addresses testing the ALT. There are cases where a Map-Reply is returned from a 'lig' request, but the user does not really know how much of the mapping infrastructure was tested. When an ITR sends a 'lig' request to its Map-Resolver for a destination EID, the Map-Resolver could also be configured as a Map-Server, and if the destination EID is for a site that registers with this Map-Server, the Map-Request is sent to the site directly without testing the ALT, because the Map-Server is the source of the advertisement for the site's EID-prefix. So if the Map-Reply is returned to the requesting site, you cannot be sure that other sites can reach the same destination EID. If a Map-Resolver is used that is not a Map-Server for the EID-prefix being sought, then the ALT infrastructure can be tested, exercising the Map-Resolver, the traversal of the ALT, which tests BGP-over-GRE, and the Map-Server. It is recommended that users issue two 'lig' requests sending Map-Requests to different Map-Resolvers. A LISP-ALT Router can also be deployed as an ALT looking-glass node, with BGP peering sessions with other ALT Routers where it injects no EID-prefixes but learns the ones advertised by others and by Map-Servers, and it is configured as a Map-Resolver that 'lig' users can point at.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two implementations: one as a router command, and one as a small program you can run anywhere with an address in the locator space. Both let you set how many probes to send and how long to wait between them. The RFC also warns that a successful answer does not prove the whole system works, because the reply may have come straight from your own Map-Server without travelling the shared infrastructure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The use of 'lig' does not affect the security of the LISP infrastructure, as it is simply a tool that facilitates diagnostic querying. The security properties of the LISP infrastructure itself are described in the LISP, LISP+ALT and Map Server Interface documents.

'lig' does, however, provide easy access to the information in the public mapping database. It is therefore important to protect the mapping information for private use. This can be provided by disallowing access to specific mapping entries, or by placing such entries in a private mapping database system.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool itself does not weaken LISP, but it does make the public mapping database easy to read. If some of your mappings are private, keep them out of the public database or restrict who can look them up.
